I am 63 years old, and I have farmed the flat land of Quzhou County for over four decades. My father taught me the basics, but because I finished high school — more schooling than most of my generation — I have always paid attention to the county extension station’s bulletins and the seed packages’ instructions. At my age, I do not chase the highest-risk crops. My back is not what it used to be, and hiring labor for picking cotton or pruning stevia costs too much and strains the household budget. I also want a system that lets me use my small walking tractor and the local combine services, so I can manage the fields without exhausting myself.

This is early spring; my winter wheat went into the ground last October after rotary tillage. I have 8 mu of good irrigated land on the North China Plain, and I will keep the entire plot in the wheat–maize rotation that has never failed me. The wheat is already established — an improved semi-dwarf variety like the ones I have been selecting for standability and grain weight — and I will topdress it with nitrogen at green-up and again at jointing, while keeping the total nutrient budget balanced. After harvest in early June, I will switch immediately to no-tillage maize using a hybrid single-cross variety. No-tillage after wheat lets me plant fast, saves diesel, and preserves the soil moisture that June heat would otherwise steal. I will irrigate both crops at the critical stages — overwinter, green-up, jointing, and filling for wheat; seedling and tasseling for maize — and I will spray pesticides only when the county plant-protection station warns of aphid or borer pressure, because over-spraying wastes money and kills the natural enemies I have learned to respect.
